# **What are the data?**
***

Before you read any files into R or Python, pause to ask what each file represents. Some files describe the original public study, some describe the balanced set of cells used for CoGAPS, and some are summaries from models that have already been run. Knowing the difference will help you avoid common mistakes, such as treating every cell as a separate participant, using a balanced modeling set to estimate original cell abundance, or reading CoGAPS weights as up- or down-regulation.

The public source data come from {{< glossary "GEO accession" display="GEO accession" >}} `GSE154386`, associated with the source study by Waickman and colleagues [@waickman2021denv1Pbmc]. The source study used a {{< glossary "10x Genomics files" display="10x Genomics" >}} 5-prime single-cell RNA-seq workflow to profile unfractionated {{< glossary "Peripheral blood mononuclear cells" display="peripheral blood mononuclear cells" >}}, or `PBMCs`. Unfractionated means that T cells, B cells, natural killer cells, monocytes, and related antigen-presenting cells were measured together rather than first being sorted into separate purified populations.

That mixed-cell design is useful for studying host response, but it also creates the central modeling challenge. Stable {{< glossary "Immune-cell identity" display="immune-cell identity" >}} and dynamic {{< glossary "Activity program" display="infection-response activity" >}} are mixed in the same expression matrices. Before you start importing tables, it helps to know which files describe the original study, which files describe the model input, and which files summarize model results.

## Data Files You Will Encounter

Use this table as a map for the rest of the case study. The first column names the file group, the second column explains why you will see it, and the third column warns against a common over-interpretation.

::: {.table-responsive}
| File group | What you will use it for | What not to conclude from it |
|---|---|---|
| Public source data: GEO `GSE154386` raw 10x files | Shows where the original single-cell data came from. You will not work directly with these raw files in the main lesson. | Do not interpret raw 10x files before sample labels, quality control, and gene/cell annotations have been added. |
| {{< glossary "Experimental infection cohort" display="Experimental DENV-1 challenge cohort" >}} | Gives the aligned infection days used for the main time-course question: `D0`, `D2`, `D4`, `D6`, `D8`, `D10`, `D14/15`, and `D28`. | Do not treat these three experimental participants as representing all dengue infections or all illness timelines. |
| {{< glossary "Balanced discovery set" display="Balanced discovery set" >}} | Defines the cells and genes sent into CoGAPS for the main model: 4,800 cells and 5,000 highly variable genes. | Do not use this balanced set to estimate the true abundance of PBMC populations in the full source study. |
| {{< glossary "Rank-sweep evidence" display="Rank-sweep summaries" >}} | Helps you decide how many patterns CoGAPS should learn before you inspect the selected model outputs. | Do not use the rank summaries alone to decide what any one pattern means biologically. |
| {{< glossary "Selected-model outputs" display="Selected-model outputs" >}} | Provides the model summaries you will import after the rank decision: pattern scores, gene loadings, top genes, diagnostics, and compact summary tables. | Do not read these files as proof of up/down regulation, causal mechanism, or viral tropism by themselves. |
| {{< glossary "Subject-timepoint summary" display="Subject-timepoint summaries" >}} | Organizes pattern scores by participant and infection day so you can follow temporal trajectories. | Do not treat these summaries as a substitute for a larger cohort or independent validation. |
| Compact-rank comparison files | Lets you compare the selected model with a smaller stable model as a sensitivity check. | Do not treat the compact comparison as the main model for the case-study interpretation. |
| {{< glossary "Pseudobulk directionality" display="Directionality tables" >}} | Helps you ask whether selected top genes are higher or lower relative to baseline after a pattern has been identified. | Do not use these tables to claim that PBMCs are directly infected by virus. |
| {{< glossary "Natural infection cohort" display="Natural infection files" >}} | Gives biological context and possible material for an extension beyond the main time-course lesson. | Do not use these files for the main aligned day-by-day discovery question. |
| Large files for rebuilding the workflow | Stores raw archives, preprocessed objects, model objects, checkpoints, and sweep outputs for people who want to rebuild the analysis. | You do not need these large files to complete the main case-study lesson. |
:::

The timeline labels use `D` for experimental study day. For example, `D0` is day 0, `D10` is day 10, and `D14/15` combines samples collected around days 14 and 15.

## How the Files Fit Together

The case study starts with public single-cell data, but you will mostly work with smaller files derived from it. Those smaller files are included so you can focus on understanding the analysis rather than rerunning every long step.

First, cells and genes were filtered, labeled, and organized into the balanced discovery set. Then CoGAPS was run on that prepared dataset. The files you import later are mostly summaries of those runs: rank-selection summaries, pattern scores, gene weights, subject-timepoint summaries, and directionality tables.

The larger raw files, model objects, and checkpoints are kept separately so the workflow can be rebuilt or checked later. You do not need to regenerate them before analyzing the included tables.

## What One Row Means

Rows change meaning from file to file. A row might be one cell, one subject at one day, one gene linked to one pattern, or one model diagnostic. Read each table with its row meaning in mind; otherwise it is easy to treat cell-level information as if it were subject-level evidence.

::: {.table-responsive}
| File group | What one row means | How you will use it | Common mistake to avoid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-cell expression matrices | One matrix connecting cells and genes. | Used to create the CoGAPS model input. | Losing track of whether rows are cells or genes. |
| Discovery cell-score files | One discovery-set cell with sample labels and CoGAPS pattern scores. | Visualizing how patterns appear across cells. | Treating many cells from one participant as many independent people. |
| {{< glossary "Subject-timepoint summary" display="Subject-timepoint summaries" >}} | One participant, one infection day, and one pattern. | Following temporal trajectories across repeated samples. | Ignoring that subject-level summaries are better for time-course claims than raw cell counts alone. |
| {{< glossary "Gene loading" display="Gene-loading" >}} and top-gene tables | One gene's contribution to one CoGAPS pattern, or one gene in a ranked top-gene list. | Asking what biology might define a pattern. | Treating a high CoGAPS weight as up-regulation or down-regulation. |
| Pattern summary tables | One CoGAPS pattern. | Comparing how strongly patterns relate to time, broad cell identity, or response scores. | Treating pattern labels as biological names before checking the evidence. |
| Diagnostic traces and metrics | One saved model-check value or one run-level summary. | Checking whether a model run behaved as expected. | Treating model diagnostics as biological findings. |
:::

::: {.definition_box}
:::: {.definition_box_header}
Independence and repeated sampling
::::
:::: {.inner_block}
Single cells are not independent {{< glossary "Biological replicate" display="biological replicates" >}}. Many cells come from the same subject at the same experimental day. You will use cell-level summaries to visualize patterns, but biological interpretation should also consider subject-level trajectories and repeated sampling over time.
::::
:::

## Balanced Discovery Set

The CoGAPS model in the main lesson was fit to a balanced discovery set. Balanced means each experimental timepoint contributes the same number of cells to the model.

In this case study, the discovery set contains 4,800 cells and 5,000 highly variable genes, with 600 cells contributing to each experimental timepoint. This makes temporal pattern comparison easier, but it also means these files should not be used to estimate the true abundance of PBMC populations in the full source study.

You will inspect the discovery-set composition in **Data Exploration**, then return to the preprocessing decisions that created the discovery set in **Data Wrangling**.

## Columns You Will See Often

You do not need to memorize every column name now. Use this table as a reference when the first imported tables appear in **Data Import** and **Data Exploration**.

::: {.table-responsive}
| Column or term | Meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `subject` | Experimental participant identifier, such as `Subject2`. | Links cells back to the biological person sampled over time. |
| `sample_id` | GEO sample identifier for a specific sample. | Tracks the source sample used to build the discovery set. |
| `cohort` | Source-study cohort label, such as experimental or natural infection. | Keeps the main discovery cohort separate from optional extension data. |
| `timepoint_merged` | Display label for the experimental day, such as `D0`, `D10`, or `D14/15`. | Defines the temporal axis used in figures and summaries. |
| `day_merged_numeric` | Numeric version of the timepoint, with `D14/15` represented as 14.5. | Lets plots and summaries order the time course correctly. |
| `broad_cell_type` | Broad immune-cell identity, such as `T_cell`, `Monocyte`, or `B_cell`. | Helps distinguish cell-identity structure from infection-response activity. |
| `n_cells` | Number of cells in a group. | Shows how much cell-level evidence contributes to a summary. |
| `fraction` | Proportion of cells in a timepoint or group. | Helps compare cell composition across days. |
| pattern-score columns | CoGAPS pattern scores in the selected-model files. The number of columns depends on the rank chosen in Data Import. | Larger values mean stronger activity of a pattern in a cell or group. |
| `pattern` | Pattern label used in long-format summaries. | Lets you compare results pattern by pattern. |
| `gene` | Gene symbol in a pattern or directionality table. | Connects model patterns to biological interpretation. |
| `weight` | CoGAPS gene loading for a pattern. | Larger values indicate genes that contribute more strongly to that pattern. |
:::

Later sections introduce additional columns such as `eta_timepoint`, `eta_broad_cell_type`, `log2FC`, `direction`, and IFN-score correlation when those values become useful for a specific research question.

## Where the Large Files Fit

Some files needed to rebuild the workflow are too large or time-consuming for the main lesson. These include the raw GEO archive, preprocessed objects, model objects, checkpoint files, and full sweep outputs. They are listed in `data/artifact_manifest.json` and explained in the Full Reproduction Guide. In the main lesson, you will use the smaller included files to understand the analysis without rerunning every long step.

:::{.think_question}

Checkpoint
::::
::::{.inner_block}
Which file would help you answer each question?

1. Why was one value of rank `K` chosen?
1. Which patterns change across infection days?
1. Are monocytes truly more abundant in the original source study?
1. Are selected top genes higher or lower relative to baseline?

<details>
<summary>Show answer</summary>

Use rank-sweep summaries for the rank decision. Use subject-timepoint summaries and visualization-ready pattern tables for temporal patterns. Do not use the balanced discovery set to estimate true cell-type abundance in the original source study, because it was intentionally balanced for modeling. Use directionality tables to ask whether selected top genes are higher or lower relative to baseline.

</details>
::::
:::
